pages.body:
Walk around your school compound or home and look closely at the soil where plants are growing well, and soil where nothing seems to grow. What do you think makes the difference?

- Just like people need food to grow strong, plants need nutrients from the soil to grow well.
- List any materials you know that farmers add to soil to help their crops grow.

Just as your body needs nutrients from food to grow and stay healthy, plants need nutrients too. Plants absorb most of these nutrients from the soil through their roots. When soil does not naturally hold enough nutrients, farmers and gardeners add extra nutrients to help their crops grow well.

> **DEFINITION** **Plant nutrient:** a substance that a plant needs, in the right amount, in order to grow, develop and stay healthy. **Fertilizer:** any substance, natural or manufactured, that is added to soil or plants to supply nutrients and improve growth.

The nutrients that farmers add to soil come from two main sources.

[[img:ilez942x0]]
[[img:i5fqcs9u1]]

| **Source** | **Where it comes from** | **Examples** |
|---|---|---|
| Organic nutrient sources | Materials that come from living things, such as plants and animals | Farmyard manure, compost, green manure, poultry droppings |
| Inorganic nutrient sources | Chemical fertilizers manufactured in a factory | Urea, muriate of potash, single superphosphate, ammonium sulphate, and compound fertilizers such as NPK |

parts.a: Organic: farmyard manure, compost, green manure, poultry droppings. Inorganic: urea, muriate of potash, single superphosphate, ammonium sulphate, NPK.

pages.body:
> **DEFINITION** **Organic nutrient source:** a plant nutrient that comes from the remains or waste of living things, such as manure or compost. **Inorganic nutrient source:** a plant nutrient made up of manufactured chemical compounds, such as fertilizer bought from a shop.

Not every inorganic fertilizer contains all three main nutrients. Some, such as urea or muriate of potash, supply mainly one nutrient. Others, called compound fertilizers, such as NPK fertilizers, are blended to supply nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K) together. Every fertilizer bag is labelled with numbers, such as 15-15-15 or 23-10-5, showing the amount of each nutrient it contains. These numbers are not always equal, and they are not the same for every fertilizer.
> **Always read a fertilizer bag's label carefully. The three numbers on it show exactly which nutrients, and how much of each, that particular fertilizer supplies.**

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Applying Plant Nutrients in the Field

pages.body:
Imagine you are given a bag of compost and a bag of chemical fertilizer, and asked to use them on the same small garden bed. Would you use the same amount of each? Would you apply them the same way?

- Think about the physical appearance of compost compared to a granular fertilizer.
- Which one do you think a plant could absorb more quickly?

Organic and inorganic nutrient sources look and behave differently, and this affects how each one should be applied to plants in the field, such as in a school garden.

**Organic nutrient sources**
- Bulky and need to be applied in large quantities.
- Release their nutrients slowly, over weeks or months.
- Usually spread over the field and mixed or ploughed into the soil before planting.
- Improve the structure of the soil and help it hold water.

**Inorganic nutrient sources**
- Concentrated, so only small quantities are needed.
- Dissolve quickly and release nutrients fast.
- Applied by broadcasting, placement near the roots, or dissolving in water.
- Do not improve soil structure, and using too much can harm plants.

There are several methods farmers use to apply nutrient sources to their crops, depending on the crop, the nutrient source, and the equipment available.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Applying Plant Nutrients in the Field (part 2)

pages.body:
| **Method** | **How it is done** |
|---|---|
| Broadcasting | Scattering the nutrient source evenly over the whole field by hand or machine, usually before or during planting. |
| Placement (side or band placement) | Placing the nutrient source in a narrow band beside or close to the row of plants, a short distance from the roots. |
| Ring method (circular placement) | Placing the nutrient source in a ring around a plant, usually at the edge of its canopy where the feeder roots are found. Commonly used for fruit trees and other tree crops. |
| Drilling | Placing seed and fertilizer together in the same row at the time of sowing, using a special seed-cum-fertilizer drill. Common on larger, mechanised farms. |
| Foliar application | Dissolving a small amount of fertilizer in water and spraying it directly onto the leaves of the plant, which absorb it quickly. Useful for correcting a nutrient shortage fast. |
| Fertigation | Dissolving water-soluble fertilizer in irrigation water so that nutrients are delivered to the plant's roots at the same time as watering. |

A small school garden will usually rely on broadcasting, placement and the ring method, since these need no special machinery or irrigation equipment.

> **Applying too much inorganic fertilizer at once can burn a plant's roots. Organic manure is gentler and safer to over apply, but slower to act.**

questions.q: Name six methods of applying plant nutrients to a field, and describe one of them in your own words.

parts.a: Broadcasting, placement, the ring method, drilling, foliar application and fertigation. For example, broadcasting is scattering the nutrient source evenly over the whole field.

questions.q: Name four methods used to apply plant nutrients to a field.

parts.a: Any four of: broadcasting, placement, the ring method, drilling, foliar application, fertigation.

questions.q: A gardener wants her vegetables to absorb nutrients quickly before the growing season ends. Which type of nutrient source should she choose, and how should she apply it?

parts.a: An inorganic fertilizer, because it dissolves quickly and releases nutrients fast. She could apply it by foliar spraying, placement near the roots, or dissolved in water (fertigation).

ideas.t: It dissolves quickly and releases nutrients fast
Apply by foliar spraying, placement or fertigation

pages.body:
- Plants absorb nutrients from the soil through their roots to grow well.
- Plant nutrient sources are grouped into organic sources, which come from living things, and inorganic sources, which are manufactured chemical fertilizers.
- Organic sources include farmyard manure, compost and green manure. Inorganic sources include urea, muriate of potash and compound fertilizers such as NPK.
- Organic sources are bulky, release nutrients slowly, and improve soil structure. Inorganic sources are concentrated, release nutrients quickly, and do not improve soil structure.
- Nutrient sources can be applied by broadcasting, placement, the ring method, drilling, foliar application or fertigation, depending on the crop and the equipment available.
- Using too much inorganic fertilizer can harm plants, so it must be applied carefully in the correct amount.

| **Word** | **What it means** |
|---|---|
| Nutrient | A substance that a living thing needs in order to grow and stay healthy |
| Organic nutrient source | A plant nutrient that comes from the remains or waste of living things |
| Inorganic nutrient source | A plant nutrient made of manufactured chemical compounds |
| Manure | Animal waste used as an organic nutrient source for plants |
| Compost | Decayed plant and food waste used as an organic nutrient source |
| Fertilizer | Any substance, natural or manufactured, added to soil or plants to supply nutrients |
| Compound fertilizer | An inorganic fertilizer blended to supply more than one main nutrient, such as NPK |
| Broadcasting | Scattering a nutrient source evenly over a whole field |
| Placement | Applying a nutrient source close to the base of a plant |
| Ring method | Placing a nutrient source in a ring around a plant, often used for tree crops |
| Foliar application | Spraying a fertilizer dissolved in water directly onto a plant's leaves |
| Fertigation | Applying fertilizer dissolved in irrigation water |
